title: Product variants without a confusing page
metaTitle: Show the variant, and its price
excerpt: If size or color changes the product, show that version. If the choice changes the price, say so next to the choice. A buried dropdown feels like another shop.
alt: A pale room with an arched opening onto a dark sofa, a low table, and a glass vase of dried stems. The specific objects fit a piece about showing the variant the shopper will actually receive.
caption: The picture should be the option they are choosing. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When should a product page change the photograph?
faqs.answer: When the choice changes the object the shopper needs to verify, such as color or material. Swap to a frame of that variant and keep the crop stable. If you do not have the frame yet, say which color the photograph shows. A dropdown alone does not display a color.

faqs.question: Where should a variant's price appear?
faqs.answer: Next to the choice, and in the total beside the add button, updated in the same moment. If every variant costs the same, one price near the title is enough. Baymard found that shoppers abandon when they cannot see the total in time. A higher price that appears only in the cart is that problem on the product page.

faqs.question: How should unavailable variants behave?
faqs.answer: Show them as unavailable, with a plain reason, or omit them and say why. Do not let a dead combination be added to the cart. If other sizes or colors remain, they still work. If the whole product is gone, say so and do not leave the add button looking active.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Product variant ux is the page's job when one product comes in real options. If size or color changes the object, show it. If the choice changes the price, say so next to the choice. A variant buried in a dropdown feels like a different shop: the picture stays generic, the price stays still, and the buyer has to imagine the thing they will actually receive.

Twenty options do not require twenty pages. They require one page that updates honestly when the choice changes.

## Show the object the choice changes

Color changes the photograph. Size sometimes changes the photograph, when the object is visibly different and not merely a label. Material changes it. A monogram, if you offer one, changes it only if you can show the mark. When the choice changes what the eye should verify, swap the image to a frame of that variant. Keep the crop consistent so the page does not jump.

If you only have one photograph, do not pretend a dropdown is a view of the color. Say that the picture shows the clay color, and that navy is the other option, and describe navy in words. Then plan the missing frame. A shop that sells color and shows one color is asking for returns and for distrust.

Nielsen Norman Group's [research on how long people stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is a constraint on how fast that update has to be legible. Jakob Nielsen reported that people often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and that the first 10 seconds decide whether a page earns more time. The variant the visitor came for, from an ad or a recommendation, should be the one on screen when the page arrives, not the first SKU in the database. Deep-link to the variant. The first 10 seconds should be about that object.

Do not animate the swap so slowly that the old object lingers. A short cross-fade is enough, and the new image should be ready, or the reserved box should hold while it loads, without pushing the title around. The title can stay stable if it is the product name. The selected option can change beside it.

Swatches beat a dropdown for color, because the swatch is a tiny proof. Make the swatch the real color, large enough to tap, with a text label as well. Color-only swatches fail people who cannot distinguish the two browns you think are obvious. The label is the accessible name and the clarification. Selected state should be visible in more than color: a ring, a word, "Navy selected."

## Say the price next to the choice

If every variant costs the same, the price can live once, near the title, and the choice does not need to repeat it. If any choice changes the price, the price next to that choice has to change, and the total near the button has to change with it. A size that costs more, still showing the cheap price until the cart, is a different shop from the one on the product page.

Baymard Institute's [cart abandonment statistics](https://baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate) report that 12 percent of US online shoppers have abandoned an order because they could not see the total cost up front. A variant price that waits until checkout is that problem, moved one step earlier. Show the difference where the decision happens. "Large, 12 more" next to the size is clearer than a price that flickers somewhere else on the page with no explanation.

Update the button's nearby total in the same moment as the selection. If a sale applies only to one color, say so on that color, and remove the sale price when they pick another. A strikethrough that survives onto a variant that is not on sale is a pricing bug wearing a design.

Currency and unit should not change position when the number changes. A layout that shifts when "9" becomes "12" will feel broken on a phone. Reserve the width. The choice is the interaction. The page staying still is the trust.

## When a list is enough, and when it is not

A dropdown is acceptable for a long list of sizes that do not change the photograph or the price in a surprising way, if the current size is visible when the list is closed and the options are real words. Even then, a row of sizes is usually better up to about eight options, because the choices are visible without a second gesture. A dropdown that contains "Small / Red / Wool" as a single smashed label is a sign you have two or three options pretending to be one. Split them. Color as swatches. Size as a row. Each selection updates the image and the price according to the rules above.

Unavailable combinations should look unavailable. A red in large that you do not make should be visible and clearly not selectable, or it should be absent with a sentence. A dead option that can still be clicked, and then fails in the cart, feels like a broken shop. Disable it, say "Large is not made in red," and keep the last valid combination on screen so the photo and the price never display a product you will not sell.

Out of stock is a variant state, not a page state, when the other variants exist. The unavailable size is marked. The others still add. If every variant is gone, the page says the product is gone and offers a way to hear when it returns. The add button does not stay active. That behavior deserves its own care, and it should not contradict the variant rules you set here.

Quantity sits near the choice, with a sensible default of one. It should not reset when they change color, unless the new color cannot support the quantity, in which case you say so. Resetting quantity in silence is how a gift order becomes a single unit.

## The address of a specific variant

The URL should identify the variant that is on screen, so a shared link opens the navy large and not the default clay small. Update the address when they change the choice, without a full reload that loses their place, and without adding a history entry for every hesitant tap if that makes the back button a trap. One history entry per settled choice is enough. Test the back button. It should leave the product, or return to the previous variant they actually considered, in a way you can explain.

Title and social preview should match the variant if the variant is what you are sharing. A generic title for a specific color will be corrected by the visitor in the first 10 seconds, and some of them will leave rather than correct it. If your stack renders the page on the server, the HTML for that URL should already contain the right name, price, and image. A client-only swap after a generic shell will flash the wrong product at exactly the moment Nielsen's research says people are deciding whether to stay.

The cart line must show the same variant the page showed: name, option, price, and a thumbnail of that option. A thumbnail of the default color next to a line that says navy is the dropdown problem again, one step later. The confirmation email repeats it. The person packing the order sees it. Variant clarity is an operations tool, not only a style.

## What not to add

Do not add a variant for a marketing idea that is not a different object. "Best seller" is not a size. A badge can say it. A fake option in the selector teaches people that the selector is advertising.

Do not reset the page scroll when the image changes. Do not open a modal to pick a size if the selector fits on the page. Do not hide the price inside the modal. The page is the shop. A modal is a detour.

Keep the selector in the tab order, with a visible focus, and with a name that says color or size. A custom swatch that only works on click will fail the keyboard. The native or the carefully built control should announce the selected value. This is the same discipline as any control a person uses to commit money. The variant is the commitment.

## A check with two real options

Pick a product where color changes the photo and size changes the price, even if you have to stage one.

- The linked URL opens on that variant, with the right photo and price in the first HTML.
- Changing color changes the photo. Changing size changes the price beside the size.
- An impossible combination cannot be added.
- The cart line matches the photo and the price you just saw.
- Back does not trap them inside a stack of half-choices.
- The selector works from the keyboard, and the selected name is text, not only a swatch.

If any line fails, fix the variant before you add a related-product carousel. The carousel is a second shop. The selector is this one.

When the chosen variant is gone, the page still has a job. [Out-of-stock states that keep the sale later](/blog/out-of-stock-states-that-keep-the-sale-later) is the next piece. Say it is gone, offer a way to hear when it returns, and do not leave the add button looking alive.

The same plainness shows up in a catalog that has already been through a redesign. Browse [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works), including shop work such as Down the Cove, and look for whether the object on the page is the object you would receive. That match is the whole task.
